https://www.thetimes.com/article/greta-t.title: Greta Thunberg at 20: how the child crusader lives now
https://www.thetimes.com/article/greta-t.text:
Greta Thunberg became the most influential child alive by sitting — small and alone — outside the austere parliament buildings in Stockholm each Friday, refusing to go to lessons until the government responded to her environment policy demands. She is a former Time magazine Person of the Year, a serial nominee for the Nobel peace prize, and a global symbol — for better and for worse — of the climate crisis. But what happens when the world’s best-known school striker no longer has a school to strike from?
Thunberg, 20, graduated from secondary school in June. So far, she has celebrated with increased vigour: a final strike outside the Swedish parliament, attended by the singer Patti Smith; a meeting with Volodymyr Zelensky, the Ukrainian president; and last week, a criminal record — after she was found guilty of disobeying police orders when she blocked oil tankers at a terminal in Malmo, Sweden. It is thought to be her first conviction.
On Friday, she was in London, protesting at the department for energy security and net zero against the Rosebank oil field off the Shetland Islands. “I’m going to continue [similar tactics],” she told Channel 4, speaking of her recent, more extreme civil disobedience. “But we are not going to back down — definitely not. The climate crisis is only getting worse.”
At the same time Thunberg herself is getting older and exploring the power she can wield as an adult.
We spoke to a number of her fellow activists and friends in Stockholm about the woman they know, away from the cameras; the reluctant celebrity at the centre of one of the world’s biggest activist networks as she searches for new ways to further her causes.
Thunberg lives by herself in a friend’s apartment in Stockholm (home addresses are publicly available in Sweden and she often gets threats to her safety). She arranges her own travel by train, bus and boat, and carries her vegan food in a lunchbox. Free time is spent doing puzzles, embroidery or hanging out with her family’s two dogs, a golden retriever, Moses, and a black labrador, Roxy, as well as her horse, Freyja, which is kept outside the city and shared with other children.
At the strikes that made her name she was accompanied by the same group of people. They are all now five years older than when they started, and grappling with what that means. “Fridays for Future is not that trendy any more,” said Isabelle Axelsson, 22, one of the climate strike movement’s founding members.
“It’s harder now than a few years ago to get people’s attention,” said Falk Schroter, 21, a Stockholm design student. “People have accepted and adapted to the concept of school strikes. A lot of people do not get outraged about it as much as they used to.”
In order to appeal to children the group abstains from civil disobedience. So in the last few months, Thunberg has looked for other groups to act alongside, upping the activism ante.
Reclaim the Future is a Swedish youth group campaigning against fossil fuels. Thunberg approached them in April — and wanted to be in the thick of the action.
Henrik Green, 30, a group member, said: “Something [Greta has] come to realise — and that she’s extremely aware of — is that all sorts of groups and people want to use her in some way. She doesn’t want to be used by someone else for their interests. She wants to join and do the things she feels are necessary and right. On her own terms.”
In June, she joined Reclaim the Future members for five days of illegal blockading in Malmo. They were trained to walk out in front of a moving oil tanker and sit on the ground for two to three hours, until they were moved on by the police.
Thunberg stayed at a local activist’s home. For breakfast the team cooked vegan porridge, their requested portion sizes written up on a board, and brought bottles of water for the heat, as they sat on the tarmac in the baking sun. “She was the same as everyone else,” said Irma Kjellstrom, 20, a spokeswoman for the group. “[People] put an incredible amount of pressure on her as a person and that is not fair.”
After the protest each day, Thunberg and the activists would retire to a nearby home or community centre — where they could “hang out and take care of each other,” said Kjellstrom. “This flow of oil tankers doesn’t stop unless young people put their bodies in front of it. It’s an intense emotional experience.”
Six of the group were charged with public disorder offences, with Thunberg being the first and only case to have gone to trial.
Greta Tintin Eleonora Ernman Thunberg was born in 2003, the eldest of two girls who grew up in a flat in urban Stockholm. Her father Svante is an actor. Her mother Malena is an opera singer who finished 21st in the 2009 Eurovision Song Contest and was last week on a concert tour of the Swedish archipelago. Her sister is an aspiring actress and pop singer.
Thunberg has a photographic memory, as a child reeling off the names of capital cities and the elements of the periodic table. She found it difficult to talk to strangers and was “very isolated and very lonely”, her father has said. She attended a grammar, Franska Skolan.
Aged eight she watched a film about the amount of plastic filling the ocean and could not get it out of her head. Paralysed by fear, she stopped eating, talking and leaving the house.
Thunberg took a year off school and was ultimately diagnosed with Asperger’s, high-functioning autism, selective mutism and obsessive compulsive disorder. Latching onto the climate crisis, she persuaded her parents to become vegan and stop flying. The action, and positive changes, energised her.
After returning to school in 2018, at 15, she decided to strike outside parliament, fuelled by hot drinks, bread and jam. Within weeks, she was famous. The movement grew to engage millions of protesters in cities across the world.
Janine O’Keeffe, 59, campaigned outside parliament from the beginning with Thunberg. “When I realised what was happening [with her public persona], I broke down in tears,” she said. “I was like, we’re ruining her life. The media, the threats, the pressure. I realised that her childhood was gone. Today, she’d rather not have to do the fame, but she’s doing it for the climate.”
Thunberg, however, has said her autism has allowed her to withstand fame: She has said she does not get stage fright, does not feel the same intimidation by authority figures, does not care about being mocked and does not shy away from saying things that might make people dislike her.
In 2018, she transferred school to Kringlaskolan, in Sodertalje, a city west of Stockholm, where she was offered a four-day-a-week education so she could continue her strikes. She left in 2019 with 14 As and 3 Bs. She took a gap year, travelling with her dad, without aides, speaking at Davos and sailing to the US to speak at the UN, famously saying: “How dare you. You have stolen my dreams and my childhood with your empty words.”
After Covid, she returned to school, the eco-friendly Globala Gymnasiet, in August 2020, where people said she was initially an outsider, the other students unsure of how to act around someone so famous. The school is known for its focus on sustainability. It has an entirely vegetarian lunch menu — the only school to have one in Stockholm — and has a herb and vegetable garden, beehive and “insect hotel”. She completed her final three years, writing her social sciences thesis on Roma strategies to deal with discrimination in Sweden, according to the newspaper, Expressen, and received As in all subjects except one. It is understood she will go to university this autumn.
She accepts no speaking fees and makes no money from her campaigning. She has published No One is Too Small to Make a Difference, a collection of her speeches, and with her family Our House is On Fire, donating all royalties to environmental charities. Last year the Greta Thunberg Foundation listed zero employees this year and total assets worth 17.3 million Swedish krona (£1.3 million). The foundation awards grants to organisations and people who “work to achieve advances on climate issues”, including the International Organisation for Migration and Unicef’s work to tackle the global malnutrition crisis.
She has been applauded by Barack Obama, Leonardo DiCaprio, the Pope and the King. Donald Trump told her she had an “anger management problem”, President Putin said she was “poorly informed”. The trolling masses, have called her mentally ill and a brainwashed puppet of financier George Soros, issued endless death threats and sent excrement to her family’s home.
Last year she told The Times she had never got drunk and feels more “vulnerable” in romantic scenarios than her less famous peers. “You have power — and also, oddly, no power,” she said.
Her “best friends” are in the climate movement. The Fridays for Future Stockholm group meets every Wednesday to organise protests as well as every other week in a community centre to unwind, where they play games, have some fika (coffee and cake) and listen to a shared Spotify playlist of their favourite music: Taylor Swift, My Chemical Romance, Swedish folk music and punk.
Climate academics come to give them “street lectures” outside parliament and Thunberg is often briefed by Johan Rockstrom, co-director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, so that she is thoroughly up to date on policy and research.
“For good and for bad, she has become a face for the movement,” said her friend Falk Schroter. “And I don’t think that is what we as a movement want or what Greta has said she would want. It is much more collaborative than that.”
“Within the group she’s just one of us,” said Eva Kroschel, 22, also a member, who has a coat with “F*** the patriarchy” written across the back. “It’s kind of weird to think that she gets so much attention but at the same time we need to be aware of it and be supportive if there are uncomfortable situations. She has the group as a support system.”
Last week the court ordered Thunberg to pay 1,500 Swedish krona (£112) and an additional 1,000 krona to the fund for crime victims after her protest in Malmo. Appearing without legal representation, she told the judge: “It’s correct that I was at that place on that day, and it’s correct that I received an order that I didn’t listen to, but I want to deny the crime”. She said later: “It is absurd that those who act in line with science should pay the price for it.”

Good day, dear Times reader, and welcome to the week when the catastrophic power struggle between the “elected” war criminal Vladimir Putin and the more “freelance” war criminals of the Wagner group spilt over, unexpectedly, into British Light Entertainment and figures therein.
And not even present British Light Entertainment figures, such as “a sexy woman” from Love Island or Bradley Walsh from The Chase. No — this unexpected “Light Entertainment/Russian mercenaries intent on obliterating Ukraine” crossover concerns a figure who, due to the vagaries of time, registers as so admirably niche that until this week connoisseurs of British pop-culture ephemera would have given an admiring, “Oh! That’s a good one. Rare cut. Respect,” if you brought him up in conversation. Shall we shilly-shally no more and go straight to the headline?
“X Factor star Wagner fears he will be assassinated after getting death threats from people confusing him with murderous Russian mercenary group with the same name,” MailOnline informed us in a 1,000 per cent googlewhack of a headline.
Wagner from The X Factor. Remember him? Strong “razzy uncle on his third divorce” vibe; stupendous mullet, moustache’n’goatee situation dominating the head area. His dancing during his version of Ricky Martin’s She Bangs brought a unique combination of both “clowning” and “restraining order” to ITV1. That Wagner. Not a man you would initially expect to get drawn into a bloody international conflict between autocrats and mercenaries, or to thrive in that situation.
Well, how wrong you would be. Wagner’s response was, initially and understandably, towards the “rueful” end: “Singer Wagner Fiuza-Carrilho, 66, said he received threats to cut off his testicles,” as the first bullet point noted — something Wagner himself was, understandably, largely against.
But then the same fighting spirit that helped him to get through to the final six in series seven, only to lose in the sing-off against Mary Byrne, came shining through. “I am ready for them,” Wagner said, firmly. “I will use my martial arts.”
He went on to discuss his success on the celebrity website Cameo, where fans pay for personalised video messages from their favourite niche pop-culture figures. “During Christmas, I was doing 60 to 70 videos a day!” he boasted.
And this is, maybe, something for The Other Wagner to consider. For what is their exit plan, when this bloody war is, finally, over? Are they building up the kind of irony-driven fanbase that means they will be making “60 to 70” video messages a day, at £40 a pop, come 2033? If not, perhaps they should “reach out” to the original Light Entertainment Wagner for a few tips. In exchange they could track down the people who are threatening to remove Wagner’s Ring Cycle and “persuade” them not to. It’s all about the give and take.
Last week, it was announced that the Queen — aka Camilla Parker Bowles, for those of us still adjusting to these new titles — will not be receiving the parliamentary annuity customarily given to the monarch’s spouse. While Prince Philip raked in a useful £359,000 a year, Camilla’s hats-and-fags money will instead be provided by the sovereign grant as part of the pre-existing funding for the royal family. This hopefully means the tax payer will get a pleasant little bonus. Perhaps we can spend it on expensively dumping more used PPE in the New Forest. That would be a nice treat.
● Queen Camilla and me: meet the stylist with royal connections
I have to say, I love the idea of our new queen being, well, more economical to run. Although one doesn’t want to be too bloodless about these things, the royal family is a brand, and each of its members, to a certain extent, a product. In terms of queens, the last model we had was a tough one to follow up: the initial launch involved a mad, cinematic plot twist in which a sexy young princess became ruler of the Commonwealth, but then decades of adroit management matured Elizabeth II into “a much-loved, very expensive, high-quality heritage item”. Like a really great Smallbone kitchen, but with a crown on it.
It’s a smart move on behalf of Camilla, then, to realise her “being queen” franchise can’t hope to compete with all the glamour, scale and “100 per cent monarch, 100 per cent of the time” vibes of her mother-in-law. And that, instead, her best positioning is towards a more, well, “Royal Greggs” end of the spectrum. Cheap, cheerful and apt to prompt a heartfelt “hurrah!” when spotted by 90 per cent of the population. If Elizabeth II was a Rolls-Royce, Camilla, it seems, is cannily opting to be a Peugeot 107 or Toyota Yaris. An unobtrusive, reliable budget model, but with, one presumes, a large ashtray Sellotaped to the dashboard.
Of course, while there are many considerable downsides to Britain getting hotter — mass tree-death; rivers full of dead fish; nasal sunburn running rampant — there is one upside: for there is nothing like the joy, on a hot day, of an ice-cold Diet Coke! Mmmmm. So painfully bubbly! So sweet!
OR IS EVEN THIS PLEASURE SCREWED TOO? For last week the World Health Organisation had to add the artificial sweetener aspartame to its list of possible carcinogens — thus throwing fans of diet drinks into a panic. SOFT DRINKS GIVE YOU CANCER was very much the vibe on social media after the announcement. Diet Coke, Pepsi Max, Sprite Zero — your boys are taking one hell of a beating.
● Diet Coke may be bad for you. But not drinking it would be worse
Of course, for those who read on further, there was a softening of this witch’s curse, for it seems aspartame becomes a possible carcinogen only when consumed in great quantity. To be brisk: you would need to drink 14 Diet Cokes a day for your aspartame levels to become problematic.
Fourteen? 14? I have no knowledge, nor facts, and speak from a position of absolute ignorance, but surely no one in the world has ever drunk 14 cans of Diet Coke? For starters, who would have the time? And for mains, who would have the abdominal capacity? The carbon dioxide in 14 cans of Coke would inflate, minimum, a mid-sized paddling pool: you would be a human gasometer before can six. The bloating would end you decades before the cancer could. Exploding is a very possible outcome.
Given this, the whole “aspartame” issue is rather like the WHO giving out a health warning on smoke inhalation for people being burnt at the stake. Technically, yes, it’s a future problem — but one swiftly overtaken by current events.
Also, now I think of it, even if you were particularly physically adapted to avoid exploding, on 14 Cokes a day you’d be toothless within a year. Plus, so wired from the caffeine, your heart would stop.
I think what I’m trying to say here is that 14 daily anything is bad.
For years, the image of unions has been dominated by a post-Thatcher narrative of “surly peasants in donkey jackets being old-fashioned and unreasonable”, attempting to hold “society” hostage through disruptive collective action, before being, quite rightly, thumped by the police.
However, after recent waves of strikes by teachers, nurses, junior doctors, train drivers, airport workers, Amazon workers, the DVLA and hospital consultants, statistically, there’s more of “society” on strike than being held hostage by it, which feels, at the very least, “food for thought, vibes-wise”.
And now — an image tipping point? For as the Writers Guild of America strikes gather pace, the writers (surly, peasant-like) have now been joined around the metaphorical brazier by the actors (sexy alpha-people). At the Oppenheimer London premiere last week the entire cast walked out on the dot of 7pm, to “go and write their picket signs”, with the stars Matt Damon, Florence Pugh, Emily Blunt and Robert Downey Jr — along with the director Christopher Nolan — putting on their metaphorical donkey jackets and making them, suddenly, look quite hot.
● Hollywood strike shows we must act fast on AI
But it was news this week that really changed the face of unionisation, when it was reported that a Zoom negotiation last month between the Hollywood union Sag-Aftra and the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers was joined by Tom Cruise, who was railing against AI and unequal pay. Tom Cruise. TOM CRUISE!
Well, now actual Maverick has “gone Mick Lynch”, we are surely about to see a radical change in the image of both unions and collective action. Presumably, future negotiations will involve Cruise shouting “ONE OUT, ALL OUT, COMRADES!” while driving through a plate-glass window on a motorbike, and/or “UNITED WE STAND, DIVIDED WE BEG!” even as he throttles a F/A-18 Super Hornet up a missile-studded mountain.
In this respect, it seems the surly peasant writers of The Comic Strip were entirely prescient: 1985’s The Strike had Peter Richardson playing Al Pacino playing Arthur Scargill, and “the Welsh miners” planning to blow up a mine with a nuclear bomb. At this rate, Billy Bragg will be winning best motion picture soundtrack at the Oscars 2025, and “I’M NOT A SCAB!” will be the new “bursting into tears and weeping, ‘I can’t believe this is real, I have so many people to thank!’ ”.
As the summer holidays begin in earnest, one story dominates the news: that going on holiday might kill you. I know. If it’s a British holiday, you are looking at probable Death by Beach Poo. This week, 80 per cent of Cornish beaches were hit with a “raw sewage alert” — meaning East Looe Beach could now be, well, East Loo Beach, and Mousehole now, essentially, “Arsehole”. If you fancy a massive dose of E. coli with your afternoon swim, Britain’s privatised and shambolic water companies have provided a magnificent faecal feast for us all. And, as seems likely, should we have to renationalise them, at a cost of a mere squillion pounds for Thames Water alone!
But in a painful “out of the bedpan and into the actual fire” scenario, if you fly away from the newly titled Great Shitain for some plop-free European holiday bliss, things don’t look any better — as the “heat bombs” of Cerberus and Charon have hit the Mediterranean. Should you venture onto a beach any further south than Calais, chances are, you won’t be covered in dung, but you will fry.
“Europe’s punishing heatwave set to hit record high,” the Financial Times reported, as temperatures verged on 50C in Spain.
● ‘It feels like you’re dying’: at the heart of Europe’s heatwave● Why is it so hot in Europe? The heatwave explained
Of course, while more than 529 million people permanently live in the affected areas, British coverage of the heat bomb — in which huge swathes of Spain and Greece have been consumed by wildfires, sparking serious speculation that within the next decade parts of the Med will become unliveable — has been, well, very British. The main headlines have been about British tourists fainting in the streets of Rome; British tourists being unable to visit the temporarily closed Acropolis; and British tourists being warned that the heat is such a “shock to the system” that they might have to spend most of their fortnight abroad in their air-conditioned hotel bedroom, sadly watching EastEnders via a VPN.
The British tabloid coverage of the crisis has continued the tradition firmly established with the 1940s headline “FOG IN CHANNEL: CONTINENT CUT OFF”. To wit: however international a problem, the primary lens must always be: “Might this, in any way, affect or inconvenience anyone from Godalming?” Hence global warming — Arctic ice-melts! American crop failure! — is getting its biggest-ever UK coverage, on the basis of “Armageddon disrupts some all-inclusive buffets, if you go Over There”.
This is because, thankfully, global warming knows Britain isn’t “part of the world”, but is BRITAIN — entirely separate from “abroad” — and so just won’t ever be involved in something that is so vile and unpleasant.
OR WILL IT? For this week, a study by the University of Oxford — who have unpatriotically presumed “global” warming will affect Britain, after all — suggested that Britain is one of the countries that will have to do the most adapting, in the next 20 years or so. Our buildings are designed to keep heat in; we have minimal air conditioning; we have a lot of glazing; and we all own at least one wool-based M&S suit. TLDR: we’re going to roast.
We’re going to have to change our working hours, the study’s author, the fabulously named Dr Jesus Lizana, told MailOnline. “In southern Spain . . . It is quite common for outdoor workers in July and August to shift to an early starting hour — like from 6am to 2pm — to avoid working during the hottest hours of the day.”
Swapping 9-5 for 6-2? Are Britons actually, biologically capable of doing this? If we are to have a Mediterranean-style “siesta” at 3pm, for starters, this means the end of the Great British Tea Break — no point in pumping yourself full of Yorkshire Gold and a KitKat at 2pm if the resultant caffeine spike leaves you sleepless and restless just as Tipping Point starts.
And if we then start having dinner at 9pm, continental-style, we’ll still be in the delightful seaside tavernas of Ramsgate, Pwllheli and Grimsby when Match of the Day starts — which seems like a greater threat to British identity than “wokedom”, drag queens and Gareth Southgate taking the knee combined.
Yes: sadly, no matter how many times you say it, “take back control” doesn’t allow us to take back control of global weather crises. We can’t Brexit our way off this planet. I guess we either actively engage in all the stuff scientists are begging us to do to combat climate catastrophe — or we become more continental. A true, John Bull patriot, then, would start voting for the Green Party. Interesting times.
